description: DevHouse is a team of six passionate innovators participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 in Dushanbe, Tajikistan. We are developing an intelligent platform to harmonize MODIS and VIIRS satellite data, analyze fire hotspots, and visualize wildfire activity. Our mission is to turn complex NASA data into meaningful insights and help protect our planet through technology, innovation, and teamwork.
summary:
We built FIREPULSE to help people explore when and where satellites detect fire activity. The web app uses MODIS and VIIRS observations from NASA FIRMS. It places detections on a common grid and counts how many cells recorded a hotspot each UTC day. The calendar compares monthly activity across sensors and applies a correction only where it improves agreement on a separate period.

Users can select a country or a map area, compare months with their historical median when enough data is available, open detections on the map, and export results as CSV. We used Tajikistan as our pilot area. The app also displays recent observations worldwide and expands its historical coverage as the archive loads.

FIREPULSE helps researchers and land managers spot unusual months and decide where to investigate further. The calendar shows how many days of data were available for each sensor.
details:
FIREPULSE is a web app that connects a global 3D map of satellite hotspots with a historical fire activity calendar. Users can select a country, compare a month with earlier years, and open that month’s detections on the map. For individual observations, the app shows the satellite, detection time, coordinates, confidence, and fire radiative power. Users can also export the data as CSV.

MODIS and VIIRS observe Earth at different resolutions and overpass times, so their detections can produce different totals for the same area. FIREPULSE places both datasets on a shared 0.02° grid and counts each cell once per UTC day when it contains a hotspot. This gives both sensors a common unit of activity. In the Tajikistan pilot, we fitted a VIIRS adjustment using data from 2013–2022 and evaluated it on 36 later months. The mean absolute monthly gap between the sensors fell from 22.64 to 3.68 active cell-days after adjustment.

To try it, select Tajikistan, open Calendar, choose 2025, and click March. The harmonized estimate is 22.62 active cell-days, compared with a historical March median of 9.50. Both sensors had data for all 31 days. This workflow helps researchers and monitoring teams identify unusual months and see where to investigate. The calendar shows coverage and flags provisional data. Satellite detections are thermal anomalies that may need confirmation on the ground.

We used Python for data preparation, Go for the API and data ingestion, PostgreSQL with PostGIS for geospatial storage, and React, MapLibre GL JS, Three.js, and Leaflet for the web interface.
